claims.text: The multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy forms thermally stabilized protective oxide films on its phase surfaces.
Mechanical wear removes protective oxide films at eutectic interphase boundaries.
Interphase boundaries become active sites for accelerated galvanic corrosion after their protective films are removed.
The constituent phases have inherent electrochemical-potential differences that create local galvanic cells when fresh metal is exposed.
Locally enhanced corrosion weakens interphase cohesion.
Corrosion-weakened interfaces increase susceptibility to further wear.
Wear-assisted depassivation and corrosion-assisted interface weakening establish a positive degradation feedback loop.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion produce greater total degradation and higher weight loss than corrosion alone at the same temperature.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion produce more pronounced wear tracks than the corrosion-only baseline.
Simultaneous wear and corrosion produce deeper localized corrosion pits at interphase regions than the corrosion-only baseline.
The proposed coupling should dominate only when the applied wear rate exceeds the oxide-film reformation rate.
If wear remains below the oxide-film reformation threshold, accelerated coupled degradation may not dominate.
An environment insufficiently aggressive to support galvanic corrosion after film removal may prevent the proposed coupling from dominating.

A controlled comparison should use identical specimens at the same elevated temperature, with simultaneous abrasion and corrosion in one group and corrosion alone with the oxide retained in the other.
Weight loss, interphase-boundary microscopy, pit depth and distribution, and wear-track profilometry can be used to evaluate the proposed degradation process.

The hypothesis is falsified if the combined-exposure and corrosion-only groups show no statistically significant difference in interphase degradation, overall weight loss, or pit depth while oxide-film condition is controlled.
